title: Recurring Decimals and Fraction Conversion
description: Recognize repeating decimals and derive reduced fractions for pure and mixed recurring decimals.
approach: Recognize and notate a repeat → derive pure recurring conversion → handle prefixes and whole parts → verify and apply.
sourceScope: R.S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude for Competitive Examinations, Chapter 3: recurring-decimal definitions and conversion rules on printed page 70; solved examples 17-18 on printed pages 72-73; objective patterns on recurring-to-fraction conversion in the chapter exercise and answer section.
opening:
A recurring decimal has a digit or block of digits that repeats forever. A bar over the repeating block marks exactly which digits recur. Before converting, identify whether repetition starts immediately after the decimal point or after a non-repeating prefix.

This distinction determines the denominator. A pure recurring block uses as many 9s as repeating digits. A mixed recurring decimal uses those 9s followed by as many zeroes as there are non-repeating digits. We will derive both rules so the denominator is meaningful rather than a memorized pattern.
recap: Identify the complete repeating block first. For a pure recurring decimal with k repeating digits, write the block over k nines and reduce. For a mixed recurring decimal, subtract the integer made from the non-repeating prefix from the integer made by writing the prefix and one repeat block; use k nines followed by as many zeroes as prefix digits. Separate any whole-number part, reduce, then verify by reversing the conversion. A terminating decimal has no infinite repeating block and uses a power-of-ten denominator instead.

lessons.text:
A decimal is recurring when a digit or fixed block repeats without end. The bar shows the repeating part: 0.̅3 means 0.3333…; 0.̅27 means 0.272727… . If the written digits stop without a repeat mark, the decimal is terminating, such as 0.375. Do not infer that a finite printed string continues forever.

A pure recurring decimal repeats immediately after the decimal point. A mixed recurring decimal has one or more non-repeating digits first, then a repeating block. The boundary between those portions controls the later conversion.
lessons.remedy: Look for the bar or an explicit ellipsis. 0.375 ends and is terminating; 0.̅45 repeats 45 from the first decimal place and is pure recurring.

q.prompt: Which number is a pure recurring decimal?
hints: Pure means the repeat begins immediately after the point.
Only one choice marks an infinite repeating block.
q.explanation: 0.̅45 means 0.454545…; the repeating block starts at the first decimal place. The other written decimals terminate.

hints: A terminating decimal has finitely many digits and no continuing repeat.
Read the bar as an instruction that the marked digits recur forever.
retry.explanation: 0.625 is a finite decimal. The other choices indicate repeating digits.

lessons.text:
The repeating block is also called the period. Count the digits in that block, not the total digits shown in a calculator approximation. For example, 0.̅27 repeats the two-digit block 27; it is not the same as 0.2̅7, where only 7 repeats after a non-repeating 2.

Notation prevents ambiguity. When reading a bar, say the non-repeating prefix first, then name the full block that repeats. This will later tell you how many 9s and zeroes belong in the denominator.
lessons.remedy: Read the bar carefully: 0.̅27 has a two-digit period, 27. In 0.2̅7, the prefix is 2 and the one-digit period is 7.

hints: The bar is placed over the digit 7 only.
The 2 before it is a non-repeating prefix.
q.explanation: The decimal means 0.2777…: 2 is the prefix and 7 repeats.

retry.prompt: How many digits are in the repeating block of 0.̅142?
hints: Count the digits under the bar.

lessons.text:
Derive the pure recurring rule by shifting the decimal until the repeating tails line up. Let x = 0.̅6 = 0.6666… . Then 10x = 6.6666… . Subtract the first equation from the second: 9x = 6, so x = 6/9 = 2/3. The infinite tails cancel because they are identical.

For a one-digit repeat, multiplication by 10 shifts one full period. Reduction to lowest terms is still required; 6/9 and 2/3 have the same value, but 2/3 is simplified.
lessons.remedy: If x = 0.666…, then 10x = 6.666…. Subtracting gives 9x = 6, so x = 6/9 = 2/3.

q.prompt: Convert 0.̅8 to a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Let x = 0.888… and compare 10x with x.
q.explanation: 9x = 8, so x = 8/9, already in lowest terms.

retry.prompt: Convert 0.̅3 to a fraction in lowest terms.

lessons.text:
If a pure repeating block has several digits, multiply by the matching power of ten so one full block shifts past the point. For x = 0.̅27 = 0.272727…, 100x = 27.272727… . Subtracting x leaves 99x = 27, so x = 27/99 = 3/11. Two repeating digits produce two 9s.

For a three-digit block, shifting three places produces 999x on subtraction. In general, a k-digit pure block is the integer made by the block divided by k nines, followed by reduction.
lessons.remedy: For x = 0.272727…, multiply by 100 because the block has two digits. Then 100x − x = 27, so 99x = 27 and x = 27/99 = 3/11.

q.prompt: Convert 0.̅27 to a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: The period has two digits, so compare 100x and x.
The first fraction is 27/99; reduce it.

retry.explanation: For a pure three-digit period, 0.̅142 = 142/999. This fraction is already reduced.

lessons.text:
The block may begin with zeroes. Those zeroes are part of the period and must be counted when choosing how many 9s to use. For 0.̅067, the period is 067, so write 67/999, not 67/99. The leading zero in the block does not change the numerator's integer value, but it does contribute to the block length and denominator.

A quick check is to compare sizes: 67/999 is about 0.067, matching the first digits of the recurring decimal. A denominator of 99 would give about 0.677, a clear scale error.
lessons.remedy: Count all digits under the bar, including the leading zero. The block 067 has length three, so use denominator 999: 67/999.

hints: The repeated block is 067, which has three places.
q.explanation: The block 067 gives numerator 67 and denominator 999: 67/999.

retry.prompt: What denominator structure is used for the pure repeat 0.̅004?
hints: Count the three digits in 004, including the zeroes.
retry.explanation: The period 004 has three digits, so its denominator is 999; the fraction is 4/999.

lessons.text:
A mixed recurring decimal has a finite prefix before the period. To remove both parts, compare two shifted forms. For x = 0.1̅6 = 0.1666…, 10x = 1.666… and 100x = 16.666… . Subtract: 100x − 10x = 15, so 90x = 15 and x = 15/90 = 1/6.

The denominator has one 9 for the one repeating digit, followed by one 0 for the one prefix digit: 90. The numerator is 16 − 1, the integer formed by prefix plus one repeat digit minus the prefix alone.
lessons.remedy: For 0.1666…, subtract the shifted values 16.666… − 1.666… = 15. Thus 90x = 15 and x = 1/6.

q.prompt: Convert 0.1̅6 to a fraction in lowest terms.

retry.prompt: Convert 0.2̅3 to a fraction in lowest terms.

lessons.text:
For a longer non-repeating prefix, append one full repeat block to the prefix digits to form the first integer, then subtract the prefix integer. The denominator contains as many 9s as repeating digits, followed by as many zeroes as prefix digits.

For 0.23̅4, the prefix is 23 and the one-digit period is 4. The numerator is 234 − 23 = 211; the denominator is 900. Thus the fraction is 211/900. Check that it is near 0.2344…, as the original decimal suggests.
lessons.remedy: There are two prefix digits and one repeating digit. Compute (234 − 23)/(9 followed by 2 zeroes) = 211/900.

hints: One repeat digit and two prefix digits give denominator 900.

retry.prompt: Convert 0.12̅3 to a fraction in lowest terms.

lessons.text:
When the repeating block has more than one digit, use one 9 for each repeating digit, then append zeroes for the prefix length. For 0.2̅35, the prefix is 2 and the period is 35. The numerator is 235 − 2 = 233; the denominator is 990. Therefore 0.2̅35 = 233/990.

This rule comes from shifting until the repeating tails line up: 100x − 10x cancels the common tail. It is not a rule to put every displayed digit over a power of ten; that would represent a terminating approximation instead of the exact recurring value.
lessons.remedy: The prefix has one digit and the period has two. Subtract 2 from 235 and use denominator 990: 233/990.

lessons.text:
For a mixed number with a whole-number part, convert only the decimal part and then combine. For 3.̅142857, write 3 + 0.̅142857. The six-digit period gives 142857/999999 = 1/7, so the value is 3 + 1/7 = 22/7.

Reducing the recurring part before adding the whole number keeps the arithmetic clear. If the final answer is requested as an improper fraction, combine using a common denominator; if a mixed number is accepted, state it explicitly.
lessons.remedy: Separate 3.̅142857 into 3 + 0.̅142857. The recurring part is 142857/999999 = 1/7, so the total is 22/7.

lessons.text:
Verify a converted fraction by reversing the reasoning or by checking its size and initial digits. For example, 1/6 = 0.1666…, which matches 0.1̅6. The exact fraction and recurring decimal represent the same value; a finite display such as 0.167 is only an approximation.

After conversion, simple arithmetic may be performed with the fractions. Convert each recurring decimal first, then use ordinary fraction operations. Keep the conversion step visible so that the repeat pattern is not mistaken for a terminating decimal.
lessons.remedy: Check the fraction against the decimal pattern. A fraction such as 1/6 has decimal expansion 0.1666…, matching one fixed digit after the prefix 1.

hints: Convert the pure repeats to 6/9 and 1/9.
